lessons.title: The Sector Rotation Clock: Where the Model Comes From and How It Works

body.text: Sector rotation is not a theory about which sectors are good. It is a theory about when each sector's earnings are most sensitive to the phase of the cycle, and therefore when the market is most likely to reward it.

children.text: Chapters 1 and 2 taught you to place the economy on the cycle. This chapter answers the question every investor actually cares about: which sectors tend to lead in each phase, and why? We start with the sector rotation clock itself, where it came from, what it claims, and the economic mechanics that make it work. Then we translate it into NSE sectoral indices, and flag where India does not fit the textbook.
Where the Model Comes From

body.title: Three Frameworks Behind the Sector Rotation Clock

events.title: Sam Stovall's sector rotation model
events.description: Published in the Standard & Poor's Guide to Sector Investing, it mapped US sector leadership to stages of the business cycle and popularised the idea that the market, and sector leadership, turns ahead of the economy.

events.title: The Merrill Lynch Investment Clock
events.description: A report led by Trevor Greetham that divided the cycle into four phases using two variables, growth relative to trend and the direction of inflation, back-tested on US data from 1973.

events.title: Fidelity's business cycle approach
events.description: Fidelity's asset allocation research maps sector performance to four phases, early, mid, late cycle, and recession, and presents the results as probabilities rather than rules.

children.text: All three frameworks were built on US data. Keep that in mind throughout this chapter; Chapter 4 tests how much of it survives contact with Indian markets.
The Classic Clock: Four Phases, Four Sets of Leaders

Fidelity's version is the easiest to map onto the four phases you already know. Its early cycle corresponds to our recovery, mid cycle to expansion, late cycle to slowdown, and recession to contraction.

body.caption: Fidelity's business cycle sector patterns (US data since 1962)
headers: Sectors that have tended to outperform

cells: Consumer discretionary, financials, real estate, industrials
Information technology; no single category outperformed more than half the time

body.text: Look at the mid cycle row. It is the longest phase, yet no single category outperformed the market more than half the time. Rotation signals are strongest at the turns, early cycle and recession, and weakest in the long middle. That is a useful warning against constantly shuffling sectors during an extended expansion.

children.text: The Investment Clock: Adding Inflation
The Merrill Lynch Investment Clock adds a dimension the simple four-phase cycle lacks: inflation. That matters in India, where food and crude oil shocks can push inflation up in any phase.

cells: Cyclical value, such as oil and gas

children.text: The clock is read clockwise: a typical boom and bust moves from reflation to recovery to overheat to stagflation and back. The report itself stressed that it is a framework for thinking, not a real-time trading rule, and that cycles often skip phases or move backwards.
Why Sectors Rotate: Four Mechanics
The clock is only useful if you understand why it works. Four economic mechanics drive most of the pattern.
1. Operating Leverage

markDefs.definition: The degree to which operating profit changes in response to a change in sales. Companies with a high share of fixed costs have high operating leverage: small changes in revenue produce large changes in profit, in both directions.

children.text: Businesses with high fixed costs, such as cement plants, steel mills, airlines, and capital goods makers, see profits swing far more than sales. That is
operating leverage
. It is why cyclical stocks can double early in a recovery on modest sales growth, and why they get crushed in a downturn.

body.caption: EBIT = earnings before interest and tax, a measure of operating profit
Same sales, very different profit sensitivity (₹ crore)

body.title: Measure Operating Leverage
body.prompt: Using the table, Company A's EBIT rises by 50% when sales rise by 10%. What is Company A's degree of operating leverage?
body.explanation: DOL = 50% divided by 10% = 5. Every 1% change in sales moves operating profit by about 5%, in both directions. Company B's DOL is 20% divided by 10% = 2. In a recovery, Company A's profits accelerate far faster, which is why high operating leverage sectors lead early in the cycle, and why they fall hardest when the cycle turns.

children.text: 2. Interest Rate Sensitivity

Some sectors feel every move in rates. Lenders such as banks, NBFCs, and housing finance companies see their funding costs, loan demand, and bad loans shift with the rate cycle. Borrower-heavy sectors such as real estate and autos depend on EMI affordability for their customers. And highly indebted companies see interest costs rise and fall with policy. These sectors tend to lead when the RBI starts cutting and lag when it starts hiking.
3. Commodity Price Linkage

Metals, mining, and upstream oil and gas earn more when commodity prices rise, which usually happens late in an expansion as demand runs into capacity limits. Commodity users, such as paints, tyres, and FMCG, often see the opposite: their margins get squeezed when input prices rise and recover when input prices fall.
4. Demand Elasticity and Pricing Power

People keep buying toothpaste, medicines, and electricity in a downturn, but they postpone cars, flats, and holidays. Sectors selling necessities have stable, low-elasticity demand, which makes them defensive: less exciting in a boom, but far more resilient when growth slows.

children.text: Translating the Clock to India

Here is how the classic phases map to NSE sectoral indices you can actually track. Treat it as a starting hypothesis, which the next three lessons refine sector by sector and Chapter 4 tests against real data.

Falling rates, operating leverage off a low base
Industrials, technology, materials as capex builds

Capex cycle, credit growth, capacity utilisation

Late-cycle commodity prices, then demand stability

body.title: Nifty 50 sector weights, as of 31 July 2026 (%)

children.text: The index you benchmark against has its own built-in sector bet. With financial services at over 36% of the Nifty 50, a rotation into or out of banks and financials moves the whole index. A portfolio that underweights financials is making a large active rotation call, whether its owner realises it or not.

body.text: India does not map neatly onto a US-built clock. Indian IT services earn most of their revenue abroad, so they respond more to US and European demand and the rupee than to the Indian cycle. Oil marketing companies are exposed to government fuel pricing decisions, not just crude prices. PSU banks and defence stocks can re-rate on government policy and ownership. And India's growth cycle rarely includes a true recession. Lessons 3.2 to 3.4 deal with each of these.

body.title: Go deeper: why the clock is a probability map, not a timetable

children.text: Markets move first. Because stocks discount the future, sector leadership often shifts months before the economic phase officially changes. By the time the data confirms a recovery, early cycle leaders may have already made most of their move.
Phases are uneven. Fidelity's US data puts the mid cycle at about three years and recessions at under one. A strategy that rotates every few months is fighting that asymmetry.
Cycles skip steps. A recovery can stall straight back into slowdown, and an external shock can jump the economy from expansion to contraction without a gentle late cycle.
Within-sector differences are large. In a slowdown, a debt-free FMCG leader and a leveraged discretionary retailer are both "consumer", but they behave very differently.
Valuation can overwhelm the clock. A defensive sector that is already expensive going into a slowdown may not outperform, because the market has priced in its safety.
Practice

body.title: Read the Investment Clock
body.question: Growth is running above trend and inflation is rising, with the RBI starting to worry about overheating. According to the Investment Clock, which asset class and equity style have historically tended to do best in this phase?
options: Commodities and cyclical value, such as oil and gas
body.explanation: Above-trend growth with rising inflation is the Overheat phase. Demand is pushing against capacity, commodity prices rise, and the Investment Clock found commodities and cyclical value sectors such as oil and gas tended to do best. Bonds suffer as inflation and rate expectations rise.

body.title: Name the Mechanic
body.textWithBlank: A cement company's operating profit rises 40% when its sales rise 8%, because most of its costs are fixed. This amplification is called operating ___.
body.explanation: Operating leverage means fixed costs amplify changes in sales into bigger changes in profit. Here the degree of operating leverage is 40% divided by 8%, which is 5. It is one of the main reasons cement, steel, and capital goods behave as early and mid cycle leaders.

cards.definition: Sectors whose earnings accelerate strongly as growth picks up, favoured in recovery. Examples often include technology and industrials.
Commodity and energy-linked sectors that benefit when strong growth pushes up prices, favoured in overheat. Oil and gas is the classic example.
Stable, often dividend-paying sectors such as utilities, favoured when growth slows and inflation stays high.
Businesses with steady demand and growth, such as consumer staples and pharmaceuticals, favoured when growth is weak and inflation is falling.
Rate sensitive and high operating leverage sectors: financials, autos, real estate, and consumer discretionary.
Low elasticity, low debt sectors: consumer staples, health care, and utilities.

body.title: Apply the Clock to a Scorecard
body.scenario: Your business cycle scorecard from Lesson 2.4 reads expansion, with a strong level score. But manufacturing PMI is starting to cool, CPI inflation has risen for three months and is above the RBI's 4% target, the 10-year bond yield is up half a percentage point over the year, and crude oil prices are higher. The RBI is on hold with a neutral stance.
body.prompt: Where does this sit on the Fidelity cycle and on the Investment Clock, and which of the four sector mechanics would you pay most attention to?
body.modelAnswer: On the Fidelity framework this looks like a maturing mid cycle edging towards late cycle: growth is still strong, but momentum in manufacturing is fading. On the Investment Clock, above-trend growth with rising inflation places it in Overheat, a phase that has historically favoured commodities and cyclical value, such as energy, over bonds and rate sensitive sectors. The mechanics to watch are commodity linkage, because higher crude helps upstream energy but squeezes margins for input-heavy sectors like paints, tyres, and FMCG, and interest rate sensitivity, because rising bond yields and inflation reduce the chance of further RBI cuts and can weigh on real estate, NBFCs, and autos. Operating leverage matters too: if manufacturing momentum keeps cooling, high fixed cost sectors are the first to see earnings estimates cut. None of this is a trade on its own. It is a set of hypotheses to check against sector earnings trends, valuations, and relative performance, which is exactly what the rest of this course does.

body.text: This lesson is educational. The sector patterns described come from historical studies, mostly of US markets, and describe tendencies, not guarantees. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy, sell, or overweight any sector, index, or fund.

points: The sector rotation clock draws on three US-based frameworks: Stovall's 1996 sector model, the 2004 Merrill Lynch Investment Clock, and Fidelity's business cycle approach using data since 1962
Fidelity's pattern: financials and consumer discretionary lead early cycle, technology in mid cycle, energy and utilities in late cycle, and staples, health care, and utilities in recession
The Investment Clock adds inflation: reflation favours bonds, recovery stocks, overheat commodities, and stagflation cash
Four mechanics drive rotation: operating leverage, interest rate sensitivity, commodity linkage, and demand elasticity
A company with a degree of operating leverage of 5 sees profits move about 5% for every 1% change in sales, in both directions
Financial services make up over 36% of the Nifty 50 as of July 2026, so rotation in and out of financials moves the whole index
The clock is a probability map built on US data: India's export IT, policy-driven PSU and energy stocks, and rare recessions all bend the pattern
